title: Imports and Namespace
content: Imports ZMod.Basic (for 𝔽ₚ = ℤ/pℤ), Finset.Basic (finite sets), List.Basic (for scanl/partial sums), Nat.Prime.Basic (primality), and Real.Basic (for log/exp in bounds). Opens the Erdos475 namespace and Finset for notation.
mathContext: The formalization works over ZMod p, Lean's representation of ℤ/pℤ. When p is prime (via [Fact (Nat.Prime p)]), ZMod p is a field, which is essential for the additive structure underlying Graham's conjecture.

title: partialSums — Cumulative Sum Sequence
content: partialSums l computes the list of cumulative sums [a₁, a₁+a₂, ..., a₁+...+aₜ] via List.scanl (· + ·) 0, dropping the initial 0. This is the key object: the conjecture asks whether there's an ordering making these all distinct.
mathContext: The partial sum sequence s_m = Σ_{k=1}^m a_k takes values in 𝔽ₚ. For distinctness, we need t distinct elements in a field of p elements, so the constraint is non-trivial when t is not too small relative to p. The use of List.scanl is a natural functional choice for cumulative computation.

title: IsValidOrdering — Ordering with Distinct Partial Sums
content: IsValidOrdering A ordering holds when: (1) ordering.toFinset = A (same elements), (2) ordering.Nodup (no repeats in the list), (3) (partialSums ordering).Nodup (all partial sums distinct). This is the central predicate of Graham's conjecture.
mathContext: The three conditions ensure the ordering is a genuine permutation of A (conditions 1-2) whose cumulative sums are injective in 𝔽ₚ (condition 3). Note that condition 3 implies t ≤ p since there are only p elements in 𝔽ₚ. The difficulty is that different orderings of the same set can have very different partial sum collision patterns.

title: GrahamConjecture — The Main Statement
content: GrahamConjecture p states: for every non-zero subset A ⊆ 𝔽ₚ, there exists a valid ordering. This is the formal statement of Erdős Problem #475. The non-zero condition (∀ a ∈ A, a ≠ 0) excludes 0 since including 0 would make two consecutive partial sums equal.
mathContext: The exclusion of 0 is essential: if 0 ∈ A appears at position k, then s_k = s_{k-1} + 0 = s_{k-1}, violating distinctness. The conjecture quantifies over ALL non-zero subsets, not just specific ones—this universality is what makes it hard. For a random ordering, the expected number of collisions grows with t, so most orderings fail.

title: Costa-Pellegrini (2020): Small Cases t ≤ 12
content: Axiomatizes: for p > 12 and |A| ≤ 12 with A ⊆ 𝔽ₚ \ {0}, a valid ordering exists. Costa and Pellegrini verified this through exhaustive computation for small primes and theoretical reductions leveraging the structure of small subsets.
mathContext: The condition p > 12 ensures the field is large enough for the statement to be meaningful (if p ≤ 12 then |A| ≤ p-1 ≤ 11 is already small). Costa and Pellegrini (2020, Archiv der Mathematik) combined computer search for specific primes with group-theoretic arguments to extend to all primes. This was the first unconditional result beyond Graham's original t = p-1 case.

title: small_sets_have_valid_orderings
content: Wrapper theorem directly applying costa_pellegrini_2020 to show that sets of size ≤ 12 in 𝔽ₚ (with p > 12) have valid orderings. Proved by exact application of the axiom.
mathContext: This theorem repackages the axiom with a more natural parameter ordering for downstream use. It demonstrates the pattern of wrapping axiomatized results in convenience lemmas.

title: Hicks-Ollis-Schmitt (2019): Large Cases t ≥ p-3
content: Axiomatizes: for p-3 ≤ |A| ≤ p-1 with A ⊆ 𝔽ₚ \ {0}, a valid ordering exists. When A is nearly all of the non-zero field, the missing elements impose strong constraints that allow structural proofs.
mathContext: Hicks, Ollis, and Schmitt (2019, J. Combin. Des.) used the polynomial method: if A misses at most 3 non-zero elements, the valid ordering can be constructed by carefully choosing a starting element and applying the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. The case t = p-1 was Graham's original result; t = p-2 and t = p-3 require additional case analysis.

title: Graham's Original: Full Non-Zero Set
content: Axiomatizes Graham's constructive proof: for A = 𝔽ₚ \ {0} (the full non-zero set, t = p-1), a valid ordering exists. Graham gave an explicit algorithm producing such an ordering.
mathContext: Graham's original proof (1970) constructs the ordering explicitly using properties of primitive roots. If g is a primitive root mod p, the ordering g, g², ..., g^{p-1} has partial sums that can be analyzed directly. This constructive approach contrasts with the existential proofs of later results.

title: Kravitz (2024): Logarithmic Range
content: Axiomatizes: for p > 2 and |A| ≤ log p / log log p with A ⊆ 𝔽ₚ \ {0}, a valid ordering exists. This was the strongest small-side result before the rectification barrier was broken. Will Sawin independently observed the same bound.
mathContext: Kravitz (2024) used character sum estimates and Freiman's theorem to handle sets of size up to log p / log log p. The bound arises because Freiman's rectification theorem—which approximates sumsets by arithmetic progressions—loses effectiveness for larger sets in 𝔽ₚ. This 'rectification barrier' at log p / log log p was a fundamental obstacle that all additive-combinatorial methods seemed unable to surpass.

title: Bedert-Kravitz (2024): Beyond the Rectification Barrier
content: Axiomatizes: for p > 2 and |A| ≤ exp((log p)^{1/4}) with A ⊆ 𝔽ₚ \ {0}, a valid ordering exists. This is a major breakthrough: exp((log p)^{1/4}) grows much faster than log p / log log p, breaking through the rectification barrier.
mathContext: Bedert and Kravitz (2024) developed entirely new techniques that avoid Freiman's theorem altogether. Instead of rectifying sets into arithmetic progressions, they work directly with the additive structure of 𝔽ₚ using a carefully designed probabilistic argument. The bound exp((log p)^{1/4}) is super-polynomial in log p but sub-polynomial in p, leaving a substantial gap to the large-side results.

title: AlspachConjecture — Generalization to Abelian Groups
content: AlspachConjecture G states: for any finite abelian group G, every non-zero subset has an ordering with distinct partial sums. This generalizes Graham's conjecture from 𝔽ₚ to all finite abelian groups.
mathContext: Brian Alspach (University of Regina) proposed this generalization. For cyclic groups ℤ/nℤ with n composite, the conjecture is more subtle since the group has zero divisors (in the ring sense) and the additive structure is richer. The conjecture remains open even for ℤ/nℤ with n composite.

title: Graham ↔ Alspach for Prime Fields
content: Proves GrahamConjecture p ↔ AlspachConjecture (ZMod p) by direct unfolding of definitions. Both directions follow by applying the hypothesis, since IsValidOrdering unfolds to the same conditions used in AlspachConjecture.
mathContext: This equivalence is immediate from the definitions but important conceptually: it shows that Graham's conjecture for 𝔽ₚ is a special case of Alspach's more general question. The proof `constructor <;> intro h A hA <;> exact h A hA` works because both conjectures quantify identically once the group is fixed.

title: HasExplicitValidOrdering — Constructive Proofs
content: HasExplicitValidOrdering A requires a function f : Finset (ZMod p) → List (ZMod p) such that f(A) is a valid ordering of A. This strengthens mere existence to computability.
mathContext: The distinction between constructive and existential proofs is significant both mathematically and computationally. Graham's original proof was constructive, but many later results use the probabilistic method or algebraic arguments that are non-constructive. An efficient algorithm for finding valid orderings remains an open question.

title: erdos_475_summary — Combined Result
content: Combines the three main verified ranges into a single theorem: (1) small t ≤ 12 (Costa-Pellegrini), (2) large p-3 ≤ t ≤ p-1 (Hicks-Ollis-Schmitt), (3) medium t ≤ exp((log p)^{1/4}) (Bedert-Kravitz). Proved as a conjunction from the three axioms.
mathContext: The summary theorem bundles the state of knowledge on Graham's conjecture. Note that range (3) subsumes range (1) for large p (since exp((log p)^{1/4}) > 12 for p large enough), but both are included for completeness. The open gap lies between exp((log p)^{1/4}) and p-3, which is the vast majority of possible values of t for large p.
